# Investigative Report: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Software Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive assessment

The strongest public evidence supports a cascading, two-stage software-supply-chain compromise.

First, a trojanized version of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER application appears to have compromised a 3CX employee’s computer. Mandiant states that this earlier compromise was the initial intrusion vector into 3CX’s network. The attacker then used access inside 3CX to move laterally, compromise both Windows and macOS build environments, and manipulate the software-production process. The attackers subsequently distributed trojanized 3CX DesktopApp installers to customers, creating a second and much larger software-supply-chain compromise. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The 3CX installers delivered a multi-stage malware chain. On Windows, the compromised application used malicious DLL loading and embedded or overlaid shellcode to retrieve command-and-control infrastructure and download additional payloads. Mandiant identified the principal downstream components as SUDDENICON, which extracted C2 information from encrypted icon files hosted on GitHub, and ICONICSTEALER, which collected browser information. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)) Kaspersky additionally documented deployment of the modular Gopuram backdoor against fewer than ten observed machines, with a particular concentration on cryptocurrency-related organizations. ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

The public attribution is best expressed as follows: the campaign was attributed with substantial but not absolute confidence to a North Korean nexus associated with financially motivated activity, commonly described in public reporting as Lazarus, AppleJeus-related activity, or Labyrinth Chollima. Mandiant tracked the activity as UNC4736 and assessed with moderate confidence that it was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky assessed that Lazarus was likely responsible, with medium-to-high confidence. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)) These labels should not be treated as perfectly interchangeable identities. MITRE ATT&CK describes Lazarus as an umbrella designation encompassing multiple North Korean operators and cautions that shared infrastructure, personnel, malware, and tradecraft make precise subgroup attribution difficult. ([S3](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

## Scope and source assessment

This reconstruction relies primarily on the April 20, 2023 Mandiant investigation published by Google Cloud, because it provides the most detailed account of the intrusion path into 3CX and the compromise of the build environment. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)) Kaspersky’s contemporaneous analysis is important for identifying Gopuram, describing victim selection, and documenting the relationship to AppleJeus and Lazarus-associated infrastructure. ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

Google Threat Analysis Group’s March 2022 report is earlier than the 3CX incident, but it supplies relevant historical evidence concerning North Korean activity targeting cryptocurrency and fintech organizations, including the compromise of Trading Technologies’ website and the use of AppleJeus-related infrastructure. ([S4](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/)) The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore provides an official contemporaneous advisory confirming the affected 3CX versions and the malware’s credential- and browser-data-stealing capability. ([S5](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/))

Cybersecurity Dive and WIRED provide useful contemporaneous reporting on scale, detection, and victim targeting, but some of their early attribution terminology predates Mandiant’s later technical assessment. ([S6](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [S7](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/); [S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

## Reconstruction of the public evidence chain

### 1. Earlier compromise of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER

Mandiant identified a malicious installer named `X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe`, with MD5 hash `ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`, as the earlier compromised software package. The file was signed under the subject “Trading Technologies International, Inc.” and contained a signed `Setup.exe`. Mandiant reported that the installer deployed a modular backdoor called VEILEDSIGNAL through a complex loading process involving malicious DLLs, DLL side-loading, SIGFLIP, and DAVESHELL. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The evidence does not establish precisely how Trading Technologies’ software was first altered, nor does it establish the full population of X_TRADER victims. WIRED reported that Mandiant had not been engaged by Trading Technologies to investigate the original compromise. Mandiant did, however, determine that the compromised X_TRADER package was available for download from the legitimate Trading Technologies website in 2022, despite the X_TRADER platform having been discontinued in 2020. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

The important evidentiary point is not that every X_TRADER user was affected, but that the malicious package was installed on a 3CX employee’s computer. Mandiant explicitly identified malicious software downloaded from the Trading Technologies website as the initial compromise vector of 3CX’s network. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### 2. Compromise of the 3CX corporate environment

After the compromised X_TRADER software was executed on the 3CX employee’s system, the attackers obtained a foothold in the 3CX environment. Mandiant reconstructed lateral movement and credential harvesting within the organization. The attackers used a compiled version of the publicly available Fast Reverse Proxy project, commonly associated with FRP, to move laterally. Mandiant identified a file named `MsMpEng.exe`, with MD5 hash `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`, placed in `C:\Windows\System32`. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The public evidence indicates that the attackers did not simply compromise an ordinary 3CX workstation and stop there. They progressed into systems involved in software development and build operations. Mandiant states that both the Windows and macOS build environments were eventually compromised. This transition was decisive because it gave the attackers the ability to alter software that 3CX distributed to customers. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### 3. Persistence and tooling inside the build environment

On the Windows build environment, Mandiant identified a TAXHAUL launcher and a COLDCAT downloader. TAXHAUL persisted by abusing DLL search-order hijacking through the IKEEXT service and operated with LocalSystem privileges. COLDCAT generated host-identifying information, communicated with a specified C2 server by HTTP POST, and expected base64-encoded shellcode in response. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

On the macOS build server, Mandiant identified POOLRAT, a macOS backdoor that used Launch Daemons for persistence. Mandiant clarified that a sample previously described in other reporting as SIMPLESEA was, in its assessment, actually POOLRAT. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

These findings show that the attackers established persistence and command execution across multiple build platforms. The available evidence does not describe every command executed in the build environment, but it does establish that the attackers compromised the systems responsible for producing both Windows and macOS versions of the 3CX DesktopApp. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### 4. Creation and distribution of the trojanized 3CX application

The attackers then inserted malicious code into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp software. The affected Windows application versions included 18.12.407 and 18.12.416; affected macOS versions included 18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416. The Singapore Cyber Security Agency advised users and administrators of affected versions to uninstall the software, conduct antivirus scans, and hunt for indicators of compromise. ([S5](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/))

Mandiant described the affected Windows software as 3CX DesktopApp 18.12.416 and earlier. The trojanized application contained SUDDENICON, a downloader that obtained additional C2 server information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. It then used a decrypted C2 server to download ICONICSTEALER, which collected browser information. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Kaspersky described the Windows infection mechanism as involving a malicious DLL that decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`. The resulting payload extracted C2 URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository and downloaded an infostealer that collected system information and browser history. ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

The use of legitimate signing and normal software-distribution channels substantially increased the potential reach of the compromise. Cybersecurity Dive reported that 3CX claimed more than 600,000 corporate customers and more than 12 million active daily users, while Huntress reported more than 242,000 publicly exposed 3CX phone-management systems based on Shodan data. These figures describe potential exposure, not confirmed compromise. ([S6](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

### 5. Broad first-stage exposure and narrow second-stage targeting

The public evidence distinguishes between the large number of organizations that could receive or execute the compromised application and the much smaller number that received the more capable second-stage malware.

Kaspersky found Gopuram on fewer than ten infected machines in its telemetry and reported that the observed targets were cryptocurrency-related companies. It characterized the targeting as “surgical precision.” Kaspersky did not identify the victim organizations publicly and stated that it had not observed evidence of actual cryptocurrency theft in the cases it examined. ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

Gopuram was a modular backdoor capable of interacting with the victim’s file system, creating processes, manipulating services and registries, timestomping files, injecting payloads, and launching additional in-memory modules. Kaspersky identified persistence through `wlbsctrl.dll`, encrypted shellcode stored under the Windows `TxR` directory, and DLL side-loading involving `ualapi.dll` and `ncobjapi.dll`. ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

The most defensible conclusion is therefore that the campaign used the 3CX compromise for initial reconnaissance and victim selection, while reserving the full Gopuram backdoor for a small subset of high-value victims. The available sources support cryptocurrency targeting as a significant objective, but they do not prove that cryptocurrency theft was completed in every targeted case or that cryptocurrency firms were the only intended victims. ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S7](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/))

## Attribution analysis

### Mandiant’s UNC4736 assessment

Mandiant tracked the activity as UNC4736, describing it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Supporting evidence included malware and infrastructure relationships involving POOLRAT, CoinGoTrade, JMT Trading, and domains associated with cryptocurrency-focused operations. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Mandiant also identified technical similarities between the compromised X_TRADER and 3CX applications. Both used the same RC4 key, `3jB(2bsG#@c7`, and both relied on SIGFLIP and DAVESHELL-related loading methods. Both used the hard-coded cookie variable `__tutma` and AES-256-GCM encryption. These similarities provide a meaningful linkage between the earlier X_TRADER compromise and the later 3CX compromise, although shared open-source tooling alone would not prove common authorship. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### Kaspersky’s Lazarus assessment

Kaspersky attributed the campaign to Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence. Its reasoning included the coexistence of Gopuram and AppleJeus on a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency company’s network, reuse of infrastructure associated with AppleJeus, and overlap involving malware such as POOLRAT. Kaspersky also connected Gopuram’s use against cryptocurrency companies with Lazarus’s historically documented financial targeting. ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

MITRE ATT&CK lists AppleJeus as software used by Lazarus Group and describes AppleJeus as a family of downloaders embedded in trojanized cryptocurrency applications. MITRE also records Lazarus as a North Korean state-sponsored group associated with multiple aliases, including Labyrinth Chollima, HIDDEN COBRA, ZINC, NICKEL ACADEMY, and Diamond Sleet. ([S9](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/); [S3](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

### Why the attribution remains qualified

Early reporting by Cybersecurity Dive associated the attack with Labyrinth Chollima, while WIRED described the responsible actors using names including Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, or Velvet Chollima. ([S6](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two)) These labels reflect the difficulty of mapping vendor-specific names to a single operational entity. Mandiant’s own wording is more cautious: “suspected North Korean nexus cluster,” with moderate-confidence relation to AppleJeus activity. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Accordingly, this report’s conclusion is that the 3CX compromise was most reliably attributed to North Korean financially motivated activity associated with UNC4736 and AppleJeus/Lazarus-related operations. Attribution to the broad Lazarus umbrella is well supported by the public evidence; attribution to one exact North Korean subgroup is less certain.

## Findings

| Question | Answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| How was 3CX initially compromised? | Through a malicious X_TRADER package downloaded from the Trading Technologies website and installed on a 3CX employee’s computer. | High |
| How did the compromise spread? | The attackers harvested credentials, moved laterally, and compromised 3CX’s Windows and macOS build environments. | High |
| How was customer software affected? | The attackers inserted malware into signed 3CX DesktopApp installers and distributed them through normal 3CX channels. | High |
| What did the first-stage malware do? | It extracted C2 infrastructure and downloaded an infostealer that collected browser and system information. | High |
| Was the full campaign indiscriminate? | No. Broad exposure was followed by selective deployment of Gopuram to fewer than ten observed machines in Kaspersky’s telemetry. | Moderate to high |
| What victims were emphasized? | Cryptocurrency and fintech-related organizations were repeatedly associated with the campaign, although they may not have been the only targets. | Moderate |
| Who was responsible? | A North Korean nexus tracked by Mandiant as UNC4736 and linked with moderate confidence to AppleJeus-related financially motivated activity; Kaspersky assessed likely Lazarus responsibility. | Moderate to high |
| Was cryptocurrency theft proven? | The sources support cryptocurrency targeting as a likely objective, but Kaspersky reported no observed proof of completed cryptocurrency theft in the cases it examined. | Moderate |

## Contradictions and qualifications

1. **Attribution-name variation.** Public reporting used Labyrinth Chollima, Lazarus, AppleJeus-related activity, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, and UNC4736. These should be treated as overlapping or vendor-specific labels rather than proven synonyms. ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S3](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

2. **macOS evidence.** Cybersecurity Dive reported that CrowdStrike observed activity on Windows and macOS, while noting that other researchers had not confirmed the macOS activity at that time. Mandiant later confirmed compromise of the 3CX macOS build server and identified POOLRAT, but this is distinct from proving that every affected customer macOS installation executed the same payload. ([S6](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

3. **Scale versus confirmed impact.** Customer and exposed-system figures describe potential reach. They do not establish that all 600,000 customers, 12 million users, or 242,000 exposed systems were compromised. ([S6](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

4. **Objective versus outcome.** Cryptocurrency targeting is strongly supported, but the provided sources do not establish the amount of cryptocurrency stolen, or that theft occurred in the specifically observed Gopuram cases. ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

## Conclusion

The public evidence establishes a rare cascading supply-chain attack: a prior compromise of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software enabled intrusion into 3CX; the attackers then reached the 3CX build environment and used that access to distribute trojanized 3CX DesktopApp software. The first-stage payload provided broad reconnaissance and data-theft capability, while Gopuram was deployed selectively against a very small number of higher-value systems. The most credible public attribution is to a North Korean financially motivated cluster tracked by Mandiant as UNC4736 and linked to AppleJeus/Lazarus-related activity. The evidence supports that assessment strongly at the broad North Korean/Lazarus-associated level, but it does not justify treating every vendor alias as a confirmed single subgroup identity.

## References

1. Mandiant. (2023, April 20). *3CX software supply chain compromise initiated by a prior software supply chain compromise; suspected North Korean actor responsible*. Google Cloud. [url website](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

2. Kucherin, G., Berdnikov, V., & Kamalov, V. (2023, April 3). *Not just an infostealer: Gopuram backdoor deployed through 3CX supply chain attack*. Kaspersky Securelist. [url website](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

3. MITRE. (2026). *Lazarus Group, Labyrinth Chollima, HIDDEN COBRA, Guardians of Peace, ZINC, NICKEL ACADEMY, Diamond Sleet (G0032)*. MITRE ATT&CK. [url website](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/)

4. MITRE. (2025). *AppleJeus (S0584)*. MITRE ATT&CK. [url website](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/)

5. Weidemann, A. (2022, March 24). *Countering threats from North Korea*. Google Threat Analysis Group. [url website](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/)

6. Cyber Security Agency of Singapore. (2023, March 31). *Malware discovered in 3CX DesktopApp*. [url website](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/)

7. Cybersecurity Dive. (2023, March 30). *Supply chain attack against 3CX communications app could impact thousands*. [url website](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/)

8. Greenberg, A. (2023, April 3). *The massive 3CX supply-chain hack targeted cryptocurrency firms*. WIRED. [url website](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/)

9. Greenberg, A. (2023, April 20). *The huge 3CX breach was actually 2 linked supply chain attacks*. WIRED. [url website](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two)
